Family Health

Menopause symptoms: matching assessment and treatment to your needs

Updated: October 19, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Menopause can affect several parts of life at once, and one treatment rarely answers every problem. A useful consultation separates the symptoms that trouble you from conditions that need their own assessment. This guide connects the main symptom groups with appropriate treatment discussions, while keeping safety, your preferences and existing health conditions in view.

There is no single first symptom or universal timetable

Perimenopause is the transition when menstrual patterns and hormone levels change; altered periods, hot flushes, sleep or mood changes may be noticed first, but the sequence varies. Natural menopause is usually recognised after twelve months without periods when another cause or hormonal contraception does not explain their absence. Hormone levels become lower, rather than all hormone production suddenly stopping.

In otherwise healthy people aged 45 or over with typical symptoms, menopause is usually identified clinically rather than by routine hormone tests. Younger age, uncertainty, surgery, medicines or other illness can change the assessment. Symptoms can improve, persist or change after periods stop; neither a fixed end date nor genetics alone predicts your experience. List your main concerns and how they affect daily life rather than assuming every new symptom is hormonal.

Hot flushes and night sweats: comfort and effective treatment are different

Keeping comfortably cool and noticing personal triggers such as alcohol, hot drinks or spicy food may make episodes easier to manage. Regular suitable activity supports general health, but it is not an established hot-flush cure through lowering FSH or LH. Acupuncture has not shown a reliable advantage over simulated acupuncture for hot flushes, and ordinary soy foods are not equivalent to a prescribed hormone treatment.

For troublesome symptoms, discuss HRT where suitable, menopause-specific cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), and selected nonhormonal prescription options. The choice depends on your health, preferences, local availability and any required monitoring. Do not postpone an effective treatment discussion while trying a succession of supplements; the safety and evidence issues apply to the whole preparation, not just its plant name.

Breast tenderness needs appropriate relief and attention to changes

Hormonal changes may contribute to breast tenderness, but medicines, infection and other conditions can also cause pain. A well-fitting supportive bra and an appropriate painkiller or pain-relieving gel may help. Ask a pharmacist or clinician what is suitable if you have stomach, kidney or other health problems, take interacting medicines or may be pregnant. Testosterone is not a routine treatment for breast pain.

Evening primrose oil has little evidence of benefit; do not assume blackcurrant oil or another oil is a proven substitute for assessment. Arrange review for pain that does not improve. Obtain urgent assessment for a new hard lump, bloody nipple discharge, a change in breast shape or skin, or a red, hot or swollen breast, particularly with fever or shivering. Pain alone is not usually cancer, but that does not make a new physical change safe to ignore.

Vaginal dryness: choose a suitable product and distinguish local treatment

Dryness, burning or discomfort during sex may respond to a vaginal moisturiser used as directed and an appropriate lubricant during sexual activity. These products serve different purposes. Avoid perfumed washes, douching and ordinary creams or food oils inside the vagina; sesame oil is not a routine recommended vaginal treatment. Unusual discharge or bleeding needs assessment rather than being labelled dryness automatically.

Low-dose vaginal oestrogen can help genitourinary symptoms, including in some people already using systemic HRT. Its absorption into the bloodstream is minimal compared with systemic treatment, and serious adverse effects are very rare; the risks must not simply be copied from oral HRT. A personal history of breast cancer requires an individual discussion, generally starting with nonhormonal options and involving the cancer specialist when appropriate, especially during aromatase-inhibitor treatment.

Low sexual desire is not just a hormone measurement

Pain, sleep, mood, medicines, relationships, stress and how you feel about your body can all affect desire. No one needs to accept painful or unwanted sex. Treating discomfort, choosing comfortable intimacy and, if wanted, counselling or psychosexual support may help. Pelvic-floor treatment should address an identified problem; doing more Kegels is not a universal way to restore desire.

For persistent, distressing low desire associated with menopause, a clinician may consider testosterone when HRT alone has not helped, after reviewing other contributors. Licensing varies and treatment needs appropriate prescribing and review; it is not a general energy, memory or breast-pain remedy. Yohimbe or yohimbine is not a safe substitute to try independently: benefit is uncertain and serious blood-pressure, heart-rhythm and other adverse effects have been reported.

Urine leakage: identify the type before choosing treatment

Leakage with coughing or exertion, a sudden urgent need to pass urine and a mixture of both need different plans. Assessment may include a bladder history, examination with consent and urine testing. Supervised pelvic-floor muscle training is a first option for stress or mixed leakage, commonly for at least three months; bladder training for urgency or mixed leakage commonly runs for at least six weeks. Ask for instruction in correct contraction and relaxation rather than repeatedly stopping urine flow to practise.

Review caffeine and fluid intake without deliberately dehydrating yourself or banning every food. A fitted vaginal pessary may help selected pelvic-organ prolapse and needs fitting and follow-up; it is not a universal cure for leakage. Medicines may suit overactive bladder after discussion of benefits and adverse effects. Systemic HRT should not be prescribed to treat incontinence; local vaginal oestrogen may help when overactive-bladder and menopausal genitourinary symptoms coexist.

Mood changes and depression deserve different levels of care

Irritability, anxiety or low mood can accompany the transition, but a depressive illness should not be dismissed as an inevitable menopause symptom. Talk about duration, loss of interest, daily functioning, sleep, previous mental health and current stresses. Seek assessment for persistent low mood, especially around two weeks or longer, and sooner if symptoms are severe or you are struggling.

Supportive activity, rest and talking therapies can help; diagnosed depression may also need medication according to severity and preference. HRT or menopause-specific CBT can be considered for certain menopause-associated depressive symptoms, but they do not replace appropriate depression care. Do not self-treat with an herbal mixture. If you may act on self-harm thoughts or cannot keep yourself safe, seek immediate emergency help rather than waiting for a routine appointment.

Concentration and memory problems should not be assumed to be hormonal

Difficulty concentrating or remembering can occur alongside menopause symptoms, poor sleep, stress, anxiety or depression. Medicines and other medical or neurological causes may also matter. Describe whether problems are new, worsening or affecting work and ordinary tasks; persistent difficulties deserve assessment rather than an automatic diagnosis of menopause or dementia.

Sleep support, useful reminders, enjoyable learning and suitable activity can support daily functioning; puzzles are not a proven dementia treatment. Ginkgo has not been shown to prevent dementia, and evidence for cognitive benefit is inconsistent; sage or ginseng is not an established memory cure. HRT should not be started for dementia prevention. Sudden facial or arm weakness, speech difficulty or other stroke symptoms require emergency help, even if they disappear.

Sleep problems: assess the disruption, not only the hot flush

Night sweats can disturb sleep, but pain, mood, medicines, restless legs or sleep apnoea may also contribute. Mention loud snoring, breathing pauses and marked daytime sleepiness. Discuss a workable sleep routine, caffeine and alcohol timing, naps and activity in relation to your actual pattern instead of assuming one bedtime rule works for everyone. Do not drive while sleepy.

Treating relevant menopausal symptoms may improve sleep. Menopause-specific CBT can help sleep difficulties associated with hot flushes; persistent insomnia may need a specific insomnia-focused approach and assessment for another sleep disorder. Chamomile tea, passionflower or valerian products are not automatically effective or harmless sleep treatment. Check products and interactions before use, and do not let sedating remedies replace assessment.

Cholesterol needs its own cardiovascular-risk discussion

Lipid levels may change around menopause, but an abnormal result should be assessed with blood pressure, smoking, diabetes, family history and other risks. Discuss whether repeat tests or a cholesterol-lowering medicine are indicated. HRT or a phytoestrogen supplement is not a substitute for that risk assessment or an indicated statin.

Food choices focus on reducing excess saturated fat and using suitable unsaturated fats, fibre-rich foods and a varied diet; removing all animal foods, all fats or imposing a low-calorie diet is not necessary for everyone. Build appropriate aerobic and strengthening activity around health and ability. Smoking-cessation support and other sustainable changes matter more than a promise that three short exercise sessions will normalise cholesterol.

Bone health: fracture risk matters as well as calcium and vitamin D

Bone loss can occur without symptoms. Discuss previous low-trauma fractures, family history, medicines such as long-term steroids, falls and other risks; a bone-density scan or formal fracture-risk assessment may be appropriate. Earlier menopause can require a different hormone and bone-health plan. Do not wait for pain before asking about prevention if you have important risk factors.

Aim for adequate calcium and vitamin D, suitable weight-bearing and strengthening activity and fall prevention. Food intake, deficiency risk and medical conditions guide whether a supplement is needed; more is not always better. Supplements alone do not guarantee fracture prevention or replace an osteoporosis medicine when one is indicated.

Osteoporosis medicines are selected individually

Bisphosphonates are established medicines that reduce bone breakdown and are often a first treatment option; the route and suitability depend on the person. A selective oestrogen receptor modulator such as raloxifene may suit selected postmenopausal people, but its fracture benefits and clot risks differ from those of other treatments. Other medicines, including injectable options, may be appropriate for higher-risk situations or when alternatives are unsuitable.

Calcitonin nasal spray is not a universal best or routine first-choice osteoporosis treatment; European regulators recommended withdrawing this use because of long-term safety concerns. HRT can reduce fracture risk while used and may fit selected people after an individual benefit–risk discussion. Agree a long-term plan before starting bone medicines and do not stop or delay them on your own; denosumab in particular needs a planned transition if stopped.

Systemic HRT is a shared decision with a specific goal

Systemic HRT can be effective for troublesome menopause symptoms, especially hot flushes, but does not treat every possible symptom or replace assessment for another illness. With a uterus, systemic oestrogen generally needs an appropriate progestogen to protect the womb lining; after total hysterectomy, oestrogen alone is usually used. This uterine-protection rule does not automatically apply to low-dose local vaginal oestrogen. HRT itself is not contraception.

Discuss age, time since menopause, medical and family history, route, formulation, dose and ongoing need. Oral and transdermal treatment do not have identical clot or stroke risks, and combined and oestrogen-only regimens differ in breast and other risks. A history of cancer, clots, heart disease, stroke or other significant illness calls for a suitably experienced clinician. HRT should not be prescribed solely to prevent cardiovascular disease or dementia, and a blanket claim that everyone must take it or everyone must avoid it is unhelpful.

Herbal products need a review of the whole preparation

Black cohosh, wild yam, dong quai, liquorice, red clover, sage and ginseng are marketed for various menopause symptoms. Evidence and product contents vary; a possible benefit from one studied extract does not establish that a mixed supplement is effective or safe. Ordinary soy food is different from concentrated isoflavones. Supplements are regulated differently from medicines and are not automatically checked for effectiveness before sale.

St John’s wort may help some mild or moderate depression, but has important interactions, including with antidepressants, contraception and other essential medicines. Ginkgo can interact with blood thinners; reported liver injury with some black-cohosh products does not establish that the herb caused every case, but still warrants caution. Bring product names and labels to a pharmacist or clinician and avoid combining preparations or replacing prescribed care with them.

Agree priorities, review treatment and recognise warning signs

Choose the problems you most want help with and ask what benefit to expect from each option, when to review it and what side effects need advice. Menopause treatment is commonly reviewed after about three months and then at least annually, with earlier review for problems; the plan should change with your needs. Keep recommended screening up to date. Bleeding after established menopause needs checking even once or in a small amount, rather than being assumed to be dryness or a familiar hormone effect.

Seek urgent same-day advice for blood in urine, even if small or uncertain, or urinary symptoms with fever, shivering, flank pain or important risk factors such as diabetes or immune suppression. A new hard breast lump, nipple or skin change also needs urgent assessment. Get emergency help for tight or squeezing chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, fainting or loss of consciousness, stroke signs or immediate danger of self-harm; do not drive yourself. These are not symptoms to wait out as a normal menopause transition.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Bring a short list of symptoms, periods, medicines and supplements; choose the problems you want to address first and ask which need separate assessment.

Ask what each treatment targets, whether it is local or systemic, what risks apply to your history and when it should be reviewed.

Keep bone and cardiovascular prevention, recommended screening and warning-symptom advice in the plan; do not replace indicated care with supplements.

How BeMama can help

A symptom record can help you describe sleep, hot flushes, mood, bleeding and the effect on daily life. BeMama cannot diagnose menopause, depression, osteoporosis or another cause of symptoms, or select a hormone or supplement regimen. Recording must not delay urgent assessment.

When to seek help

Get emergency help for tight or squeezing chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, fainting or loss of consciousness, stroke signs or immediate danger of self-harm; do not drive yourself. Seek urgent same-day advice for blood in urine, even small or uncertain, and for urinary symptoms with fever, shivering, flank pain or diabetes or immune suppression. New hard breast lumps, nipple or skin changes need urgent assessment. Any bleeding after established menopause needs checking. Do not independently start or stop hormone, mood, bladder or bone medicines.

Evidence notes updated: October 19, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Menopause symptoms vary; a symptom-based assessment is more useful than assuming every change has one hormonal cause.
  • Hot flushes, local vaginal symptoms, low desire, leakage, mood and sleep may need different treatments and sometimes different specialists.
  • Low-dose local vaginal oestrogen and systemic HRT have different purposes and risk discussions; systemic treatment usually needs uterine protection when a uterus is present.
  • Bone and cardiovascular risks need individual assessment; neither supplements nor HRT replace every indicated treatment.
  • Keep follow-up and seek care for new bleeding, urinary or breast changes; serious heart, neurological or immediate safety warnings require emergency help.

Frequently asked questions

Can HRT reduce all menopause problems?

It can help appropriate menopause symptoms, but it is not a treatment for every new complaint. The best plan may combine systemic or local treatment with separate care for depression, incontinence, high cardiovascular risk or osteoporosis. Discuss your goals, history, treatment route and need for womb protection.

What is the best medicine to prevent osteoporosis?

There is no single best option for everyone. Fracture risk, previous fractures, bone density, kidney and other health conditions and preferences guide the choice. Bisphosphonates are often used first; other medicines or HRT may fit selected people. Calcitonin nasal spray should not be treated as the default answer, and bone medicines should not be stopped without a plan.

What helps insomnia during menopause?

Assess hot flushes and other contributors such as mood, medicines, restless legs or sleep apnoea. A suitable routine and targeted CBT or insomnia treatment may help. Chamomile, valerian and passionflower are not guaranteed safe cures; ask before using sedating products and do not drive when sleepy.

What should I eat or take for mood changes?

Regular varied meals support health, but no particular food or herb reliably treats a depressive illness. Discuss persistent or disabling symptoms and suitable talking therapy or medicine. St John’s wort can interact seriously with prescriptions and contraception. Get immediate help if you cannot keep yourself safe.

Is vaginal oestrogen as risky as systemic HRT?

Low-dose vaginal treatment acts mainly locally, with minimal bloodstream absorption compared with systemic HRT and very rare serious adverse effects. It has a different purpose and does not treat hot flushes. A personal history of breast cancer still needs an individual discussion, especially during aromatase-inhibitor treatment; do not simply apply oral-HRT risk statements to every local product.

Can Kegels treat all leakage or low desire?

No. The leakage type and pelvic-floor function should be assessed, and training should be taught appropriately. Urgency may need bladder training or other treatment; a pessary has a selected role and follow-up requirements. Pelvic-floor exercises are not a universal treatment for sexual desire or pain.

Does brain fog mean I need memory supplements?

No. Sleep, stress, mood, medicines and other causes may contribute. Ongoing or worsening difficulties affecting daily life deserve assessment. Ginkgo, sage or ginseng is not an established memory cure, and HRT is not prescribed for dementia prevention. Sudden stroke-like symptoms are an emergency, even if they stop.

When should I stop calling a symptom “just menopause”?

Seek assessment when symptoms are new, worsening, persistent or affecting life. Any postmenopausal bleeding needs checking; blood in urine or new breast changes need urgent advice. Chest pressure, severe breathing difficulty, fainting or loss of consciousness, stroke signs or inability to stay safe need immediate emergency help, without driving yourself.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
